prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Hermes, Writing, Spider

outputs.L1:
It is Hermes stepping off his winged sandal. I saw the Writing Spider sitting with aplomb—his caduceus, despite the scandal, abandoned dead center in her creation, above the compost of its forfeiture, sage in location. What I wondered most—like an Android or iPad on a nightstand—was whether the sweetgum burrs and dried leaves, grown footed for the purpose of bearing away any such device or gadget as may distract him from a more pressing matter, were ornaments or accidents she interweaves in the clearly golden silk, whose subwebs are occupied by diminutive male sub-celebs holding down the fort, as she holds court, long after she vanishes, stopping short of the epiphany or apotheosis we expect from genteel arts, or a goddess.

Herse is perched on the precipice of the mattress with its luxurious bedspread, where tapestry, vis-à-vis itself, interleaves the allegory. Real gold thread weighs the covers a cherub heaves to turn down for the lovers. Would that the same, in his wings, might tip the scales, and with tears put salt in these mythical tales by sinking level with us—l’enfant in the room ...

“Who thereupon did rende the cloth in pieces every whit,  
Bicause the lewdnesse of the Gods was biased so in it.  
And with an Arras weavers combe of Box she fiercely smit  
Arachne on the forehead full a dozen times and more.”
outputs.L2:
Hermes appears to be descending from his winged sandal. I noticed the Writing Spider poised confidently at the very center of what she had made, suspended above the compost heap. Even his caduceus, in spite of the disgrace, has been left behind there like some Android phone or iPad forgotten on a bedside table. What I kept asking myself was whether the sweetgum seed balls and the dry leaves woven into the distinctly golden strands were intentional decorations or merely chance inclusions. Her web’s lower layers are occupied by tiny male hangers-on, minor celebrity figures, keeping the place secure while she presides there—and remaining long after she is gone.

The whole scene seems to halt just before the revelation or divine transformation we tend to anticipate from refined art, or from a goddess. Herse sits at the edge of the bed, near the lavish coverlet, where the woven design folds the allegory back into itself. Actual gold thread makes the bedcovers heavy, so heavy that a cherub must strain to turn them down for the lovers. If only that same weight, caught in his wings, could tip the balance; if only tears could season these old myths with salt by bringing the child in the room down to our level.

Then comes the old account: “Thereupon she tore the cloth completely to pieces, because the gods’ indecency was so partial and corrupt within it. And with a boxwood comb used by tapestry weavers, she struck Arachne hard on the forehead a dozen times or more.”
outputs.L3:
Hermes appears in the poem through the familiar symbols of his divinity: a winged sandal and the caduceus. Yet these emblems do not create a scene of confident mythic authority. Instead, the caduceus is abandoned, and the god’s presence feels distracted, displaced, or incomplete. Hermes seems less like a commanding messenger of the gods than a figure out of place, his sacred objects separated from their proper function. This unsettled image prepares the reader for a world in which classical myth has been loosened from its traditional grandeur and relocated into a stranger, more intimate setting.

At the center of this setting is the Writing Spider, positioned in the middle of her web like both an artist and a sovereign. Her materials are not merely silk but sweetgum burrs, dried leaves, and strands of gold, which she weaves into a complex creation. The web becomes a deliberate work of art, made from fragments of the natural world and transformed through her labor. Its beauty depends on patience, design, and the spider’s power to shape discarded or ordinary things into something intricate and meaningful.

The web is also portrayed as a kind of court. Around the spider’s creation are small male figures who maintain and preserve it, even after she disappears. Their presence suggests a social or political order built around her artistry, as though her work has created a realm that continues to function in her absence. The spider is therefore not only a maker but also the central authority of this miniature world. Her web holds together aesthetic, domestic, and courtly meanings at once.

The poem’s imagery gains much of its force from the contrast between mythic grandeur and modern life. Hermes and the caduceus belong to the world of divine allegory, but they appear alongside objects such as an Android or an iPad. This juxtaposition brings ancient myth into an ordinary bedroom setting, making the divine seem oddly contemporary and familiar. The sacred and the mundane occupy the same space, suggesting that myth has not vanished but has migrated into modern rooms, technologies, and private experiences.

The reference to Arachne deepens this tension between art and divine power. In classical myth, Arachne was a gifted weaver whose work exposed the lewdness, injustice, and partiality of the gods. Her punishment was not simply for arrogance but for making art that revealed uncomfortable truths about divine behavior. By recalling Arachne, the poem places the Writing Spider in a lineage of female artists whose creations challenge authority. Her web, like Arachne’s tapestry, becomes more than decoration: it is an act of witness, criticism, and imaginative power.
outputs.L4:
The text explores myth, art, and distraction by weaving together figures and images that at first seem to belong to different worlds: Hermes, the messenger god; Arachne, the mortal weaver who challenged Minerva; and a real “Writing Spider,” whose web becomes both natural object and artistic surface. Through this interlacing, the piece creates a dense collage in which classical mythology, visual description, bodily experience, digital technology, and ordinary debris all occupy the same field. The result is not a straightforward retelling of myth, but a layered meditation on how meaning is made when sacred stories and everyday materials are caught in the same web.

Hermes enters as a figure of movement, mediation, and mischief. As the god of messages, crossings, thefts, and sudden transformations, he presides over the text’s restless form. The writing itself behaves hermetically: it slips from one subject to another, translates image into language, and turns attention away from any single stable center. Hermes is not simply a mythological ornament; he becomes a principle of composition. The text moves like a messenger through time, carrying fragments from antiquity into the present and letting them collide with contemporary objects such as Androids and iPads. These playful anachronisms prevent myth from feeling distant or sealed away. Instead, the ancient world appears as something still active, still tangled in the devices and distractions of modern life.

Arachne, meanwhile, provides the central figure for art-making. Her story is already a story about artistic rivalry, pride, punishment, and transformation. In myth, Arachne’s weaving is so skillful that it rivals the work of the goddess herself, and her tapestry exposes the scandals and abuses of the gods. This matters because her art is not merely beautiful; it is accusatory. It reveals what divine authority would rather conceal. By invoking Arachne, the text suggests that art’s power lies not in repeating official sacred meanings, but in troubling them. The tapestry becomes a site where beauty and scandal meet, where technical mastery cannot be separated from critique.

The “Writing Spider” extends Arachne’s myth into the natural world. Its web, marked by distinctive patterns, appears almost like script or inscription. The spider seems to write, though not in human language; it produces a form that invites interpretation without yielding a single clear message. This ambiguity allows the text to blur the boundary between art and nature. Is the web a biological structure, an aesthetic object, a sacred sign, or a meaningless accident that human beings cannot help reading as meaningful? The answer is all of these at once. The spider’s web becomes a living ekphrasis, an object that demands description while resisting full translation into words.

The text’s use of ekphrasis—its intense description of visual forms—reinforces this concern with surfaces, patterns, and interpretation. Webs, tapestries, screens, and images all become related structures. Each one catches things: light, dust, insects, stories, glances, and desires. The web is not only a symbol of artistic order, but also a trap and a record of contact. It gathers whatever happens to fall into it. In this way, the text refuses to treat art as something pure or separate from the world. Instead, art is shown as a sticky, compromised, and material process. It is made out of thread, bodies, accidents, waste, attention, and interruption.

The playful references to Androids, iPads, and other modern distractions deepen this idea. These devices may seem comic or jarring beside Hermes and Arachne, but their presence is crucial. They remind us that contemporary attention is itself webbed: caught in screens, feeds, notifications, and fragments of information. The ancient tapestry and the digital screen begin to resemble one another. Both are surfaces on which images appear; both can seduce, distract, and reveal; both can expose hidden scandals while also burying us in spectacle. By placing mythology beside modern technology, the text suggests that distraction is not merely a modern failure of concentration. It is part of how perception works. We are always being pulled between the sacred and the trivial, the beautiful and the ridiculous, the meaningful and the disposable.

This is why the text’s collage-like form is so important. It does not simply argue that myth, art, and ordinary life are connected; it performs that connection. Its density, its sudden shifts, and its mixture of high and low references make the reader experience the very entanglement it describes. Hermes, Arachne, the Writing Spider, digital devices, bits of debris, and moments of visual wonder all coexist within the same woven structure. The text becomes a tapestry about tapestry, a web about webs.

Ultimately, the piece finds that sacred allegory and everyday debris cannot be separated. The divine does not appear in a pure realm above the world; it appears amid dust, insects, scandal, technology, and distraction. Likewise, ordinary material life is not empty of significance. A spiderweb in a corner, a screen in the hand, or a myth retold with comic anachronism can all become sites of revelation—not because they deliver a single divine truth, but because they expose the entangled nature of experience.

Art, then, is significant less because it grants access to some untouched sacred meaning than because it reveals how meanings are woven together. Beauty is never alone. It is bound to violence, rivalry, vanity, labor, accident, and decay. Scandal is not outside art but often at its center, as Arachne’s tapestry shows. And ordinary matter—thread, silk, dust, pixels, scraps—is not beneath interpretation; it is the very substance from which interpretation is made. The web/tapestry becomes the governing image for this vision: a fragile but intricate structure in which myth and material life, divine story and daily distraction, are inseparably caught.
outputs.L5:
Hermes, the swift-footed messenger of the gods, carried words between worlds. With winged sandals brushing the dawn, he crossed mountains, seas, and shadows, delivering secrets from Olympus to the ears of mortals. But one evening, as he rested beside an old olive tree, he noticed a tiny spider spinning a web between two silver leaves.

The spider worked with patience Hermes had rarely seen. Thread by thread, it wrote its fragile design into the air, a pattern both delicate and strong. Hermes leaned closer and smiled. “You are a writer too,” he said, “though your ink is silk and your page is the wind.”

The spider paused, as if understanding him, then continued weaving. Hermes realized that writing was not only the mark of a stylus on wax or ink upon parchment. Writing could be movement, memory, and creation. It could be a web that caught the light, a message waiting for the right eyes to read it.

From that day on, Hermes carried not only spoken words, but also the silent writings of the world: the paths of rivers, the tracks of birds, the cracks in stone, and the shining webs of spiders at sunrise. Each one told a story, and each story, like a message from the gods, deserved to be delivered.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental ekphrastic poem that collages the myth of Hermes, Herse, and Arachne with a spider web above compost, modern devices like an Android or iPad, and archaic lines from Ovid/Golding, preserving a fragmented, interleaved layout.
counterfactuals.output:
**WEB ABOVE COMPOST / WITH ANDROID LIGHT**

after a painting not yet painted  
or an iPad screen gone dim in the garden shed

---

                              the spider has hung  
                              her little hexed cathedral

over the compost bin—  
coffee grounds, onion skins, a rind of moon,  
the soft brown rumor of fruit returning

                              *No kind of living creature is there none*  
                              *but by and by is altered one to one*

Golding says this from the mulch,  
his English bristling with burrs.

---

Hermes enters as notification:

> **1 new message**  
> from: **god with winged feet**  
> subject: **Herse**

His sandals buffer in the blue air.  
He has crossed the cloud-server,  
the bright Olympus of glass towers,  
the algorithmic sheepfolds.

He sees her—  
Herse—  
standing in the temple’s upload of sunlight,

                              her name a drop of dew  
                              clinging to the camera lens.

Beside her: Aglauros, envy’s green firewall.  
Behind them: Minerva’s loom,  
already making a noise like a hard drive.

---

                              *Yet trust me not in this, but looke upon*  
                              *Arachne’s worke—*

No—  
look up.

The web above compost  
is a tablet cracked into radiance.

Each thread catches:  
gnat, ash, pollen, the last breath  
of a pear core.

Each thread says: touch screen.

Each thread says: do not touch.

---

Arachne sits in the corner  
of the Android’s black mirror,

eight-fingered,  
eight-eyed,  
scrolling through atrocities of gods:

Europa as pop-up ad,  
Leda as corrupted file,  
Danaë in a shower of paywalled gold.

She pinches to zoom.  
She weaves.  
She refuses the update.

                              *She wrought the faultes of heavenly powers*  
                              *in shapes of earthly things—*

and Minerva, blue with authority,  
strikes the device from her hands.

The glass blossoms.

The girl becomes a loading icon  
turning and turning and turning.

---

Hermes, meanwhile,  
cannot get past the door.

Aglauros sits there  
like a password mistyped three times.

Her heart:

          /stone  
          /stone  
          /stone

                              *And straight her colour faded quite,*  
                              *her blood forsooke her face—*

He touches her with the wand  
that wakes / that closes / that routes the dead.

She becomes marble latency,  
a buffering threshold.

Herse inside,  
dew-bright,  
unopened.

---

Above the compost, the spider  
tightens her sentence.

No god helps her.  
No goddess punishes.

She takes the rotten heat  
rising from potato eyes, eggshells, tea leaves,

and fastens it  
to nothing.

                              O changing bodies—  
                              O bodies changed—

The iPad on the potting bench  
reflects the web,  
reflects the hand holding it,  
reflects the hand’s small tremor.

For a second:

Hermes is the cursor.  
Herse is the unread message.  
Arachne is the network.  
Minerva is the Terms & Conditions.  
Compost is the archive.

---

Then wind.

The whole work shivers—  
not broken,  
not whole—

          a myth in strands  
          a screen in sleep  
          a god at the gate  
          a girl at the loom  
          a spider above decay

                              *all things doo chaunge,*  
                              *but nothing sure dooth perish.*

And under it, warm and dark,  
the dead leaves keep replying.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense postmodern poem in which Hermes steps off his winged sandal into a domestic bedroom scene, a writing spider becomes Arachne, and mythological tapestry imagery merges with gadgets, bedspreads, gold thread, cherubs, and compost.
counterfactuals.output:
Hermes arrives by notification:  
one winged sandal left hovering in the hall,  
the other stepped out of, casually,  
beside the laundry basket—  
god as errand, thief as afterthought,  
ankle bright with road-dust and blue LED.

In the bedroom the bedspread is already a cosmos,  
polyester firmament quilted with cherubs,  
each pink mouth blowing clouds across the seams,  
each cloud a password forgotten in sleep.  
A charger coils like a tame serpent on the nightstand.  
The phone glows: oracle, mirror, little black altar  
where thumbs sacrifice themselves to news.

Above the headboard, the writing spider hangs  
between lamp-chain and curtain rod,  
her yellow glyphs stitched on air:  
X, O, warning, weather, alphabet of hunger.  
She spins the room into margin, footnote, loom.  
Then the old crime wakes in her abdomen—  
not spider but Arachne, not web but thesis,  
not silk but argument drawn from the body.

Hermes, messenger of thresholds, grins  
and slips the room a counterfeit dawn.  
“Translate this,” he says,  
and the spider’s legs begin their furious citation:  
Leda in the duvet’s rumple, Europa in the screen-saver,  
Io lowing through the voicemail,  
Daphne pixelated into wallpaper leaves,  
Zeus everywhere—cloud backup, pop-up, gold rain  
leaking through the cheap blinds.

Gold thread needles the bedspread’s pastoral lie.  
Cherubs grow teeth. The tapestry refuses the wall  
and crawls over the radiator, the laptop,  
the half-read book face-down like a drowned bird.  
Every gadget becomes an instrument of the loom:  
router humming fate, tablet shining war,  
remote control clicking the Fates forward  
one channel at a time.

In the corner, the compost bucket exhales  
its democratic rot: coffee grounds, peels, wilted basil,  
the green afterlife of dinners and declarations.  
Arachne knots it in—  
mold as laurel, eggshell as moon,  
banana bruise as underworld bruise—  
because no myth survives without refuse,  
without the kitchen’s dark theology  
softening in a plastic pail.

Hermes bends to retrieve his sandal,  
but the sandal has become a small boat,  
then a tongue, then a golden shuttle  
darting through warp and woof.  
The bed is no longer a bed  
but a battlefield, bridal chamber, browser window,  
a museum label rewritten in lipstick:  
DOMESTIC INTERIOR WITH GOD, SPIDER, AND DECAY.

Arachne laughs in eight directions.  
Her web catches dust, desire, data,  
a loose eyelash, a receipt, Olympus in miniature.  
The cherubs plummet sweetly into compost.  
Gold thread roots in the peelings.  
Hermes lifts one bare foot, listening—  
somewhere a message fails to send,  
somewhere a goddess edits the terms of service,  
somewhere the bedroom keeps weaving  
what it was never meant to hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal literary pastiche combining classical mythology, arachnid observation, and Renaissance translation diction; include Hermes’ caduceus, Arachne being struck with a boxwood comb, and a contemporary nightstand with an iPad.
counterfactuals.output:
Lo, in the ninth hour of a sleepless house, when the lamp upon my contemporary nightstand made a small domestic moon, and beside it lay an iPad, black and smooth as Lethe under glass, I beheld a spider descend from the cornice with such grave arithmetic that my soul, being overburdened with daylight, gave itself to marvel.

She came not as a thief, but as a scholar.

Her eight feet touched the air and found it legible. She measured the void by silken parentheses, setting one thread to the lampshade, another to the brass drawer-pull, another—O prodigy!—to the very rim of that tablet wherein men now imprison lightning, letters, maps, and the faces of their absent loves. The iPad woke beneath her shadow, and a pale annunciation rose up: notifications, those lesser Mercuries, crying without voices.

Then from the corner of the room, where the wallpaper peeled like an old Sibyl’s bark, issued Hermes, nimble god, patron of errands and deceits, holding his caduceus: that wand whereon two serpents, twined in mutual argument, seemed ever about to kiss and ever to bite. His winged sandals made no sound upon the hardwood floor. He looked upon the spider’s labour, and laughed with the courtesy of a courtier who hath already stolen the king’s seal.

“Little weaver,” quoth he, in diction antique and perfumed with the dust of folios, “what web makest thou betwixt Olympus and this bedchamber of mortals?”

The spider paused. Her abdomen trembled like a dark fruit of thought. No answer came, unless thread be answer; and truly, what are words but threads troubled by breath?

Straightway the room unfolded into another age. The nightstand lengthened into a loom; the charging cord became a skein of moon-white flax; the iPad, illumined, displayed not icons but the rape of Europa, the grief of Niobe, the foam-born laughter of Venus, all translated into a hundred tongues and yet understood by none. And there, proud Arachne stood, slender as a needle, her hair bound back, her eyes bright with that perilous excellence which offendeth gods because it resembleth them.

Minerva entered not by door nor window, but by the old severity of judgment. In her hand she bore a boxwood comb, polished smooth from many vanities of women and many orderings of hair. With that same comb she struck Arachne—yea, not with thunder, nor spear, nor aegis fringed with snakes, but with the yellow boxwood teeth of domestic correction. The blow rang strangely, like a shuttle dropped in an empty chapel.

Arachne staggered, and where the comb had touched her brow there blossomed a little mark, neither wound nor ornament, but destiny. Her fingers thinned. Her speech curled inward. Her human grief gathered itself into a knot of black patience. Then was she altered: not wholly diminished, as moralists affirm, but translated—O Renaissance word, most faithful and most false!—translated from woman into spider, from voice into filament, from pride into geometry.

Hermes lifted his caduceus, and the serpents upon it leaned forth to observe her.

“Behold,” said he, “a text that crawlest.”

And indeed the arachnid, now upon my nightstand again, resumed her making. She crossed the air above the iPad with exquisite deliberation, touching each radial line, tightening each spiral, revising by instinct what no hand could draft. I, poor witness, bent near and saw how she would halt at vibrations too subtle for my mortal apprehension: the whisper of dust, the engine-hum of the sleeping city, the soft electric pulse of the tablet, wherein distant wars and recipes, prayers and advertisements, were mingled in one luminous broth.

The web enlarged. It took into itself the old myths and the new devices. Upon one strand hung Hermes’ laughter; upon another, Minerva’s wrath; upon a third, the faint grease of my thumbprint left on the iPad’s glass. The spider waited at the centre, a dark punctuation. She was not repentant. She was not triumphant. She was attention itself.

Then methought the caduceus budded leaves of boxwood, and every comb-tooth became a tiny loom, and from the screen of the iPad rose Arachne’s tapestry, scrolling without end: gods misbehaving in the margin, mortals annotating their ruin, serpents spelling commerce around a golden staff, and one small spider, practical and sublime, repairing the rent between ages.

Whereupon Hermes, being god of passages, bowed to her.

And I, being only a man in bed, afraid to break the web and more afraid to understand it, turned off the lamp. Yet still in the dark the tablet glowed; and still the spider laboured; and still the old blow of the boxwood comb sounded softly through the room, as though time itself were carding the hair of night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fractured, high-art poem with overlapping clauses and enjambed phrases about a golden orb-weaver spider, using the myths of Arachne and Hermes/Herse as an allegory for weaving, writing, eroticism, and divine scandal.
counterfactuals.output:
**Gold Thread, or: Herse at the Loom**

In the angle of eaves—  
where rain rehearses its silver handwriting,  
where dusk unbuttons  
one cloud from another—  
she hangs,

the golden orb-weaver,  
her abdomen a small sun  
caught in its own theology,

and all night draws out of herself  
a grammar of hunger,  
a radial psalm,  
each filament trembling  
with the near-arrival of wings.

Arachne, you understand,  
was never only punished—  
she was translated:

girl into spindle,  
breath into silk,  
wound into architecture,  
the body’s bright insult  
made legible to gods.

And Hermes—  
thief of thresholds,  
gold-tongued passer between chambers—  
comes crossing the lattice of air  
toward Herse,

Herse of dew,  
Herse the gleaming,  
Herse whose name beads on the grass  
like a secret the morning  
cannot keep.

What is seduction  
but a thread cast into darkness,  
what is writing  
but a web where the hand  
waits for the world to strike?

The spider knows—  
with her eight black needles,  
her lacquered patience—  
how desire must be fastened  
at points of stress,

how scandal  
requires tension,

how even a god  
caught in the wrong house  
becomes a vibration  
on someone else’s line.

Above the garden  
the moon opens its pale coin-mouth  
and says nothing;

below it, gold ropes  
burn between branch and lintel,  
a manuscript no priest  
can smooth flat,

for every clause snags  
on another clause—  
Arachne’s tapestry in the temple,  
Hermes’ hand at the veil,  
Herse startled into radiance,  
the spider writing  
and un-writing  
her own perishable law.

O artisan of appetite,  
little heretic  
with the sun sealed in your belly,

you do not distinguish  
between making and taking,  
between the kiss  
and the trap,

between the lyric  
and the fly’s last  
glittering objection.

You fling your body  
into absence  
and call the absence home.

You bind air  
until air confesses shape.

And if Athena still watches—  
cold in her helmet of sanctioned forms—  
let her watch:

this is no moral woven clean,  
no obedient cloth,

but a net of gold misread as light,  
a bed, a page, a crime  
of radiance,

where the divine stoops  
and is caught,

where the mortal girl  
keeps weaving,

where the spider,  
widowed each dawn  
by her own design,

eats the ruined script  
and begins again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**[folio 404: ARGIOPE / ARAƆHNE / AUTO-SAVE FAILED]**

In the fennel’s green apparatus the Writing Spider  
hangs head-down, an ink-drop given legs—  
black lacquer, lemon hieroglyphs,  
eight hinged calipers measuring the noon.

Her web: an orb of weather.  
Radial lines taut as harpwire,  
spiral glue beaded with dew,  
and through the center, that white torn lightning—  
the **stabilimentum**, stitched zig-zag,  
as if the air itself were trying to sign its name.

> “Lo, she that weavèd pride in silken snare,  
>  Must wear her craft upon her back for aye.”

So says the margin, browned and moth-eaten.  
So says Minerva, logging in as *Pallas_Admin*,  
downloading the girl’s defiance,  
flagging the tapestry for mythological content.

Arachne uploads a meadow: Europa, Leda,  
Danaë’s bright error—  
all gods as breach, as golden pop-up,  
as cloud with hands.  
The goddess sees the file and strikes.

**Real gold thread weighs the covers.**  
The book shuts like a jaw.

In the room—no, in the root directory—  
there is **l’enfant in the room**,  
sticky-fingered, luminous, unnamed,  
watching the spider vibrate once  
when a grasshopper blunders into syntax.

Naturalist note, corrupted:  
female *Argiope aurantia*, abdomen ovate,  
silver cephalothorax, legs paired in X posture,  
prey wrapped rapidly in silk;  
male diminutive, peripheral, occasionally consumed;  
egg sac papery, brown, urn-shaped,  
suspended among the asters like a small lost planet.

> “O mortall hand, presume not overmuch;  
>  The loom remembers every touch.”

But the page refreshes.  
But the orchard buffers.  
But the spider writes without alphabet,  
her body a stylus dipped in hunger,  
her silk a cable between leaf and leaf,  
between old punishment and today’s blue screen.

Minerva’s spear becomes a cursor.  
Ovid’s river becomes a scroll bar.  
The nymphs are cached in willow shade,  
their hair gone vine, bark, laurel, reed—  
each metamorphosis a failed escape  
rendered beautifully.

And still the Writing Spider mends the tear:  
leg over leg, code over code,  
a yellow-black priestess of late summer  
binding sunlight to the weeds.

The web says: **I was girl.**  
The web says: **I was needle.**  
The web says: **404 mother not found.**  
The web says nothing—  
only trembles when touched,

only gleams,

only holds.
